title: The Watermelon Problem
coreMove: Attention is how finite life becomes experience, so protect enough of it to let your values choose what becomes real.

exampleSpecs.audience: Hermine, an editor deciding whether a suspense loop deserves promotion
exampleSpecs.stakes: A cheap viral segment could gather attention while pushing elections, war reporting, and local duties out of view.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use the Buzzfeed watermelon case to judge attention capture as reality selection, not harmless filler.

exampleSpecs.audience: Fatima, a product lead revising how success is named
exampleSpecs.stakes: The dashboard can reward attention capture while hiding what users meant to care about.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use James Williams's freedom frame to challenge a pure engagement metric.

exampleSpecs.audience: Ludovic, a designer reviewing defaults in a social product
exampleSpecs.stakes: Small engagement prompts may train users to let the product pick reality by default.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Expose Silicon Valley engagement design as an engineered environment, not a fair willpower contest.

exampleSpecs.audience: Madeleine, a student noticing what a short diversion displaced
exampleSpecs.stakes: A trivial clip can crowd out the careful attention she meant to give a difficult text.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show that the cost of a distraction can exceed the minutes spent.

exampleSpecs.audience: Myriam, a station manager weighing a platform promotion
exampleSpecs.stakes: The campaign looks free while charging listeners in awareness, data, and redirected habits.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Treat commercial attention capture as a cost even when no money changes hands.

exampleSpecs.audience: Brian, a reader avoiding a puritanical response to distraction
exampleSpecs.stakes: Overcorrecting into total control can become another fantasy that collapses by Monday.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Keep James Williams's freedom concern without turning the lesson into app deletion absolutism.
